title: The Letter of the Palatinate
premise: In 1713, as the War of the Spanish Succession grinds toward the Treaty of Utrecht, Felix Hartwell serves as an indentured clerk to the Vanterpool Trading Company in a Rhenish port town, trained to record cargoes and forget faces. When an infant is abandoned at the countinghouse door with a sealed letter and the instruction to 'forget the face,' Felix recognizes the child's mother as a diver's daughter from her own drowned village — a woman the company's ledgers list as sold, not dead. Pursuing the truth means forging, stealing, and finally testifying: Felix must smuggle the company's own falsified indenture rolls to the Palatine commissioners arriving to arbitrate claims before the armistice freezes every debt and death into legal silence. The book ends with the letter read into the record and the child reclaimed by her grandmother's kin, while Felix, her contract voided by the commissioners' ruling, chooses to stay in the town she once measured only in exits — no longer invisible, no longer alone.
about_author: C. M. Iversen is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing merchant ledgers from the Rhine trade before turning to fiction. They write historical novels about the people history filed under 'miscellaneous.'

chapters.title: What Can Be Carried
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Establishes the countinghouse's rhythms, Felix's talent for invisibility, and her private habit of memorizing the faces she's ordered to forget. When orders come to inventory the warehouse ahead of wartime requisition, she measures every room in what can be carried. Emotional beat: competent detachment masking an old grief for her diver father, lost to the company's debts.

chapters.title: The Child at the Door
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. A November night, a knock, an infant wrapped in sailcloth, a sealed letter, and a voice in the dark: 'Forget the face.' The factor orders the child sent to the foundling registry by morning. Felix recognizes the wrapping's knotted pattern — a diver's knot from her own village. Emotional beat: the first crack in her trained indifference; she lies for the first time, hiding the child in the loft.

chapters.title: Ledgers of the Sold
chapters.summary: Alternating Felix's present with her memories of the village. Searching the company archives for the child's mother, she finds the indenture rolls altered: women listed as 'discharged' who were in fact sold downriver. The letter's seal matches the factor's private correspondence. Emotional beat: discovery curdling into dread — the company doesn't just trade goods; it trades people, and the paper says so.

chapters.title: The Factor's Arithmetic
chapters.summary: Factor Brandt's POV, rare and chilling. He suspects the clerk; he calculates the cost of silence versus exposure as easily as cargo. He offers Felix her freedom papers if the child disappears quietly. Emotional beat: the antagonist's banality — he isn't cruel, he's efficient — and Felix's realization that her invisibility was always his design.

chapters.title: A Network of Small Treasons
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. She builds an unlikely found family: Marta the tavern keeper who nursed the child, old Sander the lockkeeper who owes Felix's father a debt, and Ilse, a company laundress who can read. Together they plan to copy the falsified rolls. Emotional beat: warmth and terror entwined — belonging, Felix learns, is a liability the company will price.

chapters.title: Utrecht Moves the Deadline
chapters.summary: Ilse's POV. News arrives: the Palatine commissioners will sit in the town for six weeks only, hearing claims before the armistice voids all pending disputes. After that, the victors' historians write the record. The window is real but closing. Emotional beat: hope with a countdown — for the first time Felix has a destination, not just an escape.

chapters.title: The Copying Nights
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. By candlelight in the loft, the household copies the rolls, page by page, while the child sleeps between them. A near-discovery when Brandt audits the archive early forces Sander to forge a delay seal. Emotional beat: quiet heroism and deepening bonds — the copying becomes a vigil, a family made in stolen hours.

chapters.title: Betrayal at the Lock
chapters.summary: Sander's POV. En route to the commissioners, Sander is intercepted; the copied rolls are seized and he is arrested as a thief. Brandt now has proof of Felix's hand and threatens to hang the theft on all of them — and to register the child as company property, an asset to be sold. Emotional beat: the plan's collapse and the crushing cost of having dared to matter to people.

chapters.title: The Hearing
chapters.summary: Felix's POV, climax. Rather than flee, Felix walks into the commission hall and testifies — not from the stolen copies, which are gone, but from memory: every face, every name, every altered entry, recited from a lifetime of forced memorization. Marta and Ilse corroborate; the child, brought forward, is the living evidence the paper can't be. Emotional beat: invisibility weaponized — the clerk who was made to forget becomes the record no one can burn.

chapters.title: The Letter of the Palatinate
chapters.summary: Felix's POV, resolution. The commissioners rule the rolls fraudulent, void the indentures, and read the sealed letter into the record — the mother's dying testimony naming her seller. The child goes to her grandmother's kin upriver; Brandt is ruined by his own arithmetic. Offered passage anywhere, Felix stays, opening a small scribe's shop that keeps honest ledgers. Emotional beat: belonging chosen, not assigned — the girl who measured the world in what can be carried finally sets something down.
